claims.text: High-temperature mechanical and thermoelastic behavior in refractory high-entropy alloys is governed by the formation and evolution of a complex network of dislocations and grain boundaries.
In-situ neutron diffraction and HRTEM can reveal the proposed dislocation and grain-boundary network under high-temperature conditions.
The relevant initial refractory high-entropy alloy may have an FCC or BCC crystal structure.
The proposed characterization is conducted at temperatures up to 1000°C.
The proposed high-temperature hold time is 1 hour.
An argon or vacuum atmosphere prevents oxidation during the high-temperature experiment.
Dislocation density is a structural mediator of the mechanical and thermoelastic response.
Grain-boundary misorientation is a structural mediator of the mechanical and thermoelastic response.
Thermally activated dislocation glide changes the alloy's mechanical and thermoelastic properties.
Grain-boundary sliding changes the alloy's mechanical and thermoelastic properties.
At 800°C, the refractory high-entropy alloy will have 20% greater yield strength than the conventional-alloy baseline.
At 800°C, the refractory high-entropy alloy will have a 15% lower thermal expansion coefficient than the conventional-alloy baseline.
The baseline is a conventional alloy with similar composition but without the high-entropy effect.
Precipitates or solute atoms may affect the predicted mechanical and thermoelastic outcomes.
The hypothesis is falsified if both yield strength and thermal expansion coefficient differ by no more than 10% from the baseline at 800°C.
